analysis.investment_thesis: Central Bank of India is a government-owned PSU bank that accumulated INR ~15,000 Cr in losses from FY16-FY21 and is only now recovering — a recovery driven largely by systemic NPA resolution, not structural improvement in the franchise. Government ownership of 89.3% means capital allocation will always be directed by political objectives rather than shareholder returns.
key_strengths: Net profit has recovered strongly to INR 3,943 Cr in FY25 after years of losses, and total assets have grown to INR 5 lakh Cr
P/B of 0.82x appears cheap on the surface, offering some margin if the recovery is real and durable
Other income growing at 12.9% CAGR reflects some improvement in fee-based revenues
key_risks: ROE of just 11.4% is below my 15% threshold even after a recovery cycle — suggesting the underlying franchise has limited earning power
Revenue CAGR of only 3% over nine years means the bank has barely kept pace with nominal GDP growth, let alone grown its competitive position
Operating cash flows negative in four of the last five years, reflecting aggressive loan-book expansion financed externally — a dangerous pattern if credit quality deteriorates
red_flags: Six consecutive years of net losses (FY16-FY21) totalling roughly INR 15,000 Cr — this is not a blip but a fundamental breakdown in credit underwriting
Government (promoter) owns 89.3% — this ensures the bank will be used for priority sector mandates, directed lending, and bailouts of other PSUs, all at the cost of minority shareholders
FII holding of only 0.75% signals that informed global institutional investors have essentially no confidence in this franchise
analysis.detailed_analysis:
I have a simple rule: I do not understand banking well enough to invest in weak banks, and PSU banks in India are structurally challenged. The six years of losses at Central Bank were not bad luck — they reflected decades of poor credit underwriting, government-directed lending, and overstaffing. The current profitability is partly cyclical (low NPA provisions post-resolution) and not structural franchise improvement. There is no moat here — any savings account customer can walk next door to HDFC Bank.

At 3% revenue CAGR over nine years and ROE of 11.4%, this business does not earn its cost of capital in a sustained manner. Even the 'cheap' P/B of 0.82x could prove expensive if the NPA cycle turns again. I would rather pay a fair price for a wonderful bank — a private sector lender with superior underwriting, technology, and management — than a bargain price for a bank that destroys capital in bad cycles.
